title: Anomaly and Outlier Detection
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Anomaly and Outlier Detection ##### The ₹4.2 crore that looked perfectly normal A manufacturing group in Coimbatore monitored 340 machines with vibration sensors. Their alerting rule was a global threshold: flag any reading above 8.5 mm/s, the ISO limit for that machine class. A gearbox failed catastrophically. The vibration readings in the four weeks before failure had peaked at 6.1 mm/s — comfortably below the threshold, never once triggering an alert. Repair and downtime came to ₹4.2 crore. The signal was there. That specific machine had run at 2.1 mm/s for three years. Going to 6.1 was a tripling of its own baseline, and every one of those readings was normal *globally* and wildly abnormal *for that machine, at that load, at that time of day*. A global threshold cannot see that. Detecting it requires asking whether a value is unusual **in its context** rather than unusual in absolute terms — and that distinction organises the whole field. ##### Three types of anomaly The taxonomy determines which method can possibly work. **Point anomalies.** A single observation is unusual on its own. A ₹4.2 lakh transaction on an account that never exceeds ₹8,000. Detectable by global methods. **Contextual anomalies.** The value is normal globally but abnormal given its context — machine identity, time of day, season, user history. The Coimbatore gearbox. A ₹40,000 spend is unremarkable for a corporate account and extraordinary for a student account. **Collective anomalies.** No individual point is unusual, but the *pattern* is. A heart rhythm where every beat is within normal range but the sequence is arrhythmic. Forty small transfers of ₹49,000 each, all just below the reporting threshold. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Anomaly detection task] --> B{Which type?} B -->|Point: unusual in isolation| C[Global methods: z-score, IQR,
Isolation Forest, one-class SVM] B -->|Contextual: unusual given context| D[Condition on context first] D --> E[Per-entity baselines, residuals
from a predictive model, LOF] B -->|Collective: unusual as a sequence| F[Windowed features, autoencoders,
sequence models] ``` **Most real-world anomalies are contextual**, and most deployed systems only detect point anomalies. That gap is where the expensive failures live. The standard technique for contextual detection is to **model the expected value given the context, then flag large residuals**: ```python import numpy as np, pandas as pd # Per-entity baseline — the Coimbatore fix stats = (df.groupby(["machine_id", "load_band", "hour_band"])["vibration"] .agg(["mean", "std", "count"]).reset_index()) df = df.merge(stats, on=["machine_id", "load_band", "hour_band"], how="left") # Robust z-score within context; require enough history to trust the baseline df["context_z"] = (df["vibration"] - df["mean"]) / df["std"].clip(lower=0.05) df["contextual_anomaly"] = (df["context_z"].abs() > 4) & (df["count"] >= 50) print(df.loc[df.contextual_anomaly, ["machine_id", "vibration", "mean", "context_z"]] .sort_values("context_z", ascending=False).head()) ``` The gearbox at 6.1 against a baseline of 2.1 ± 0.4 has a contextual z-score of 10. It would have alerted weeks before failure. ##### Statistical methods Fast, interpretable, and the correct first attempt on low-dimensional data. **Z-score** assumes approximate normality: ```python z = (x - x.mean()) / x.std(ddof=1) outliers = np.abs(z) > 3 ``` Its weakness is that the mean and standard deviation are themselves corrupted by the outliers you are trying to find — a single extreme value inflates the standard deviation and masks everything else. This is called **masking**, and it makes plain z-scores unreliable on contaminated data. **Modified z-score** uses median and MAD, which are robust: ```python def modified_zscore(x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: median = np.median(x) mad = np.median(np.abs(x - median)) return 0.6745 * (x - median) / (mad if mad > 0 else 1e-9) outliers = np.abs(modified_zscore(x)) > 3.5 # Iglewicz-Hoaglin threshold ``` The 0.6745 constant makes MAD comparable to a standard deviation under normality. This is the version to reach for by default. **IQR fences** make no distributional assumption: ```python q1, q3 = np.percentile(x, [25, 75]) iqr = q3 - q1 lower, upper = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr ``` The 1.5 multiplier is Tukey's convention, chosen so roughly 0.7% of normal data falls outside. On heavily skewed data it flags many legitimate values, which is itself informative — it tells you the distribution is skewed. **Mahalanobis distance** handles the multivariate case, accounting for correlation: ```python from scipy.stats import chi2 from sklearn.covariance import MinCovDet, EmpiricalCovariance # Robust covariance — MCD resists contamination up to ~25% mcd = MinCovDet(support_fraction=0.75, random_state=42).fit(X) d2 = mcd.mahalanobis(X) threshold = chi2.ppf(0.99, df=X.shape[1]) # under normality, d² ~ chi-squared outliers = d2 > threshold print(f"{outliers.mean():.2%} flagged at the 99th percentile") ``` Mahalanobis catches something univariate methods cannot: a point where **every individual feature is normal but the combination is impossible**. Height 150 cm is fine, weight 95 kg is fine, together they are unusual. Use `MinCovDet` rather than the empirical covariance, since the latter is itself corrupted by outliers. ##### Isolation Forest Liu, Ting and Zhou's insight inverts the usual approach. Instead of modelling what normal looks like and measuring deviation, **isolate points directly** — anomalies are few and different, so random splits separate them faster. Build random trees by picking a random feature and a random split value. Anomalies end up in shallow leaves; normal points require many splits to isolate. The average path length across trees becomes the anomaly score. ```python from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest iso = IsolationForest( n_estimators=200, max_samples=256, # the paper's recommendation; subsampling helps contamination=0.02, # expected proportion — sets the threshold max_features=1.0, bootstrap=False, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1, ) iso.fit(X_train) labels = iso.predict(X_test) # -1 = anomaly, 1 = normal scores = -iso.score_samples(X_test) # higher = more anomalous print(f"flagged {(labels == -1).mean():.2%}") ``` Three properties make it the practical default. It is **O(n log n)** and scales to millions of rows. It needs **no distance metric**, so mixed feature scales hurt less than in distance-based methods. And it handles **high dimensions** better than LOF or one-class SVM. Two details worth knowing. `max_samples=256` is deliberate — the original paper found that subsampling *improves* detection by reducing swamping (normal points appearing anomalous because of crowding). And **`contamination` only sets the decision threshold**, not the model; if you have no idea, use `score_samples` and pick the threshold from a cost analysis instead. ##### Local Outlier Factor LOF measures whether a point's local density is lower than its neighbours' density. That makes it the natural choice for **local** anomalies — points normal globally but unusual within their neighbourhood. ```python from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor # Unsupervised mode: fit and predict on the SAME data lof = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, contamination=0.02, n_jobs=-1) labels = lof.fit_predict(X) scores = -lof.negative_outlier_factor_ # higher = more anomalous # Novelty mode: fit on clean data, then score NEW points lof_novelty = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, novelty=True, n_jobs=-1) lof_novelty.fit(X_train_clean) new_labels = lof_novelty.predict(X_test) ``` **The `novelty` parameter is a genuine source of confusion.** With `novelty=False` (default) you can only call `fit_predict` on the training data — there is no `predict`. With `novelty=True` you get `predict` on new data but cannot use `fit_predict`. Choose based on whether you are cleaning a dataset or deploying a detector. LOF's strength is exactly the Coimbatore scenario: a cluster of dense normal readings and a sparse region nearby. A global method sees the sparse point as within range; LOF sees that its neighbourhood density is a fraction of its neighbours'. Its weakness is the curse of dimensionality — it relies on distances, which stop discriminating above roughly 20 features. Reduce dimensions first, or use Isolation Forest. **One-class SVM** learns a boundary enclosing the normal data: ```python from sklearn.svm import OneClassSVM from sklearn.linear_model import SGDOneClassSVM oc = OneClassSVM(kernel="rbf", gamma="scale", nu=0.02).fit(X_train_scaled) labels = oc.predict(X_test_scaled) # Linear approximation for large datasets — O(n) instead of O(n²) oc_fast = SGDOneClassSVM(nu=0.02, random_state=42).fit(X_train_scaled) ``` `nu` upper-bounds the fraction of training points allowed outside the boundary. One-class SVM requires **scaled features**, is O(n²) to O(n³) in training, and is sensitive to `gamma` — which makes it a poor default despite appearing in every textbook. Use it when you have clean training data, moderate size, and a genuinely non-linear boundary. ##### Autoencoders For high-dimensional or structured data — images, sequences, wide sensor arrays — an autoencoder learns to compress and reconstruct normal data. Anomalies reconstruct badly because the network never learned their pattern. ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn class Autoencoder(nn.Module): def __init__(self, n_features: int, latent: int = 8): super().__init__() self.encoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(n_features, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, latent), ) self.decoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(latent, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, n_features), ) def forward(self, x): return self.decoder(self.encoder(x)) def train_autoencoder(X_normal, epochs=100, latent=8, seed=42): torch.manual_seed(seed) X = torch.tensor(X_normal, dtype=torch.float32) model = Autoencoder(X.shape[1], latent) opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-5) loss_fn = nn.MSELoss() loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader( torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(X), batch_size=128, shuffle=True) for epoch in range(epochs): for (batch,) in loader: opt.zero_grad() loss = loss_fn(model(batch), batch) loss.backward() opt.step() return model def reconstruction_error(model, X): model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): Xt = torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32) return ((model(Xt) - Xt) ** 2).mean(dim=1).numpy() model = train_autoencoder(X_train_normal) errors = reconstruction_error(model, X_test) threshold = np.percentile(reconstruction_error(model, X_train_normal), 99) anomalies = errors > threshold ``` The critical requirement: **train on normal data only**, or the autoencoder learns to reconstruct anomalies too and the signal disappears. If you cannot guarantee clean training data, train on the bulk and accept that heavily-represented anomaly types will be missed. Two design points. **The bottleneck must be narrow enough** to force genuine compression — a latent dimension close to the input dimension lets the network learn an identity mapping and nothing is detected. And **per-feature reconstruction error** tells you *which* dimensions were anomalous, which is far more actionable than a single score: ```python with torch.no_grad(): Xt = torch.tensor(X_anomalous, dtype=torch.float32) per_feature = ((model(Xt) - Xt) ** 2).numpy() worst = pd.Series(per_feature[0], index=feature_names).nlargest(5) print("most anomalous dimensions:", worst.round(4).to_dict()) ``` For sequences, an **LSTM autoencoder** captures temporal patterns and detects collective anomalies. For a probabilistic version with a principled likelihood, a **variational autoencoder** gives calibrated scores. ##### Evaluation with few labels The hard part. Anomaly detection usually has no labels, or a handful — and the standard metrics assume plenty. **When you have some labels**, evaluate on the labelled subset with precision-recall, never accuracy: ```python from sklearn.metrics import (average_precision_score, precision_recall_curve, roc_auc_score, precision_score, recall_score) def evaluate_detector(y_true, scores, k_values=(50, 100, 500)): out = { "pr_auc": average_precision_score(y_true, scores), "baseline_pr_auc": y_true.mean(), "roc_auc": roc_auc_score(y_true, scores), } order = np.argsort(scores)[::-1] for k in k_values: top_k = order[:k] out[f"precision@{k}"] = y_true[top_k].mean() out[f"recall@{k}"] = y_true[top_k].sum() / y_true.sum() return out for name, s in [("IsolationForest", iso_scores), ("LOF", lof_scores), ("Autoencoder", ae_scores)]: print(name, {k: round(v, 4) for k, v in evaluate_detector(y_true, s).items()}) ``` **Precision@k is usually the metric that matters**, because the operational constraint is analyst capacity. "Of the 100 alerts we can investigate today, how many are real?" is the question a fraud or maintenance team actually has. **When you have no labels**, four substitutes: **Synthetic injection.** Inject known anomalies and measure detection rate. Crude, and it only tests the anomaly types you thought to inject. ```python def inject_anomalies(X, n_anomalies=100, magnitude=5.0, seed=42): rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) X_out = X.copy() idx = rng.choice(len(X), n_anomalies, replace=False) for i in idx: j = rng.integers(0, X.shape[1]) X_out[i, j] += magnitude * X[:, j].std() * rng.choice([-1, 1]) labels = np.zeros(len(X), dtype=int); labels[idx] = 1 return X_out, labels ``` **Consensus across methods.** Points flagged by several independent detectors are more likely genuine: ```python detections = pd.DataFrame({ "iso": iso.predict(X) == -1, "lof": lof_novelty.predict(X) == -1, "mahalanobis": mcd.mahalanobis(X) > threshold, "autoencoder": errors > ae_threshold, }) detections["n_methods"] = detections.sum(axis=1) print(detections.n_methods.value_counts().sort_index()) consensus = detections.n_methods >= 3 ``` **Expert review of the top k.** Send the 50 highest-scoring points to a domain expert. Expensive, small sample, and it is real ground truth — which makes it the most valuable option. **Stability.** A detector whose flagged set changes completely across bootstrap resamples is detecting noise. ##### Choosing the threshold The score is continuous; the decision is binary. That threshold is a business decision, not a statistical one. ```python def threshold_by_cost(scores, y_true, cost_fn=400_000, cost_fp=2_000): """cost_fn: a missed failure. cost_fp: an unnecessary inspection.""" candidates = np.unique(np.quantile(scores, np.linspace(0.90, 0.9999, 500))) rows = [] for t in candidates: flagged = scores >= t fn = int(((y_true == 1) & ~flagged).sum()) fp = int(((y_true == 0) & flagged).sum()) tp = int(((y_true == 1) & flagged).sum()) rows.append({"threshold": t, "alerts": int(flagged.sum()), "tp": tp, "fp": fp, "fn": fn, "precision": tp / max(tp + fp, 1), "recall": tp / max(tp + fn, 1), "total_cost": fn * cost_fn + fp * cost_fp}) return pd.DataFrame(rows) curve = threshold_by_cost(scores_val, y_val) best = curve.loc[curve.total_cost.idxmin()] print(f"threshold {best.threshold:.4f}: {int(best.alerts)} alerts, " f"recall {best.recall:.2f}, precision {best.precision:.2f}, " f"cost ₹{best.total_cost:,.0f}") ``` In the Coimbatore case the asymmetry is extreme — ₹4.2 crore for a missed failure against a few thousand rupees for an unnecessary inspection. That ratio implies a very low threshold and a high false-positive rate, which is the correct engineering answer even though it feels wasteful. When capacity rather than cost is binding, set the threshold at the k-th highest score and report precision@k. ##### Building a production system ```python from dataclasses import dataclass from sklearn.preprocessing import RobustScaler from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline @dataclass class AnomalyDetector: """Ensemble of complementary detectors with contextual baselines.""" contamination: float = 0.02 def fit(self, X_train, context_df=None): self.scaler = RobustScaler().fit(X_train) # robust to the outliers present Xs = self.scaler.transform(X_train) self.iso = IsolationForest(n_estimators=200, max_samples=256, contamination=self.contamination, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1).fit(Xs) self.lof = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, novelty=True, n_jobs=-1).fit(Xs) self.mcd = MinCovDet(support_fraction=0.75, random_state=42).fit(Xs) if context_df is not None: self.baselines = (context_df.groupby(["entity_id", "context_band"])["value"] .agg(["median", "std", "count"])) return self def score(self, X, context_df=None) -> pd.DataFrame: Xs = self.scaler.transform(X) out = pd.DataFrame({ "iso_score": -self.iso.score_samples(Xs), "lof_score": -self.lof.score_samples(Xs), "maha_score": self.mcd.mahalanobis(Xs), }) # Rank-normalise so scores on different scales are combinable for c in out.columns: out[c + "_rank"] = out[c].rank(pct=True) out["ensemble"] = out[[c for c in out if c.endswith("_rank")]].mean(axis=1) if context_df is not None and hasattr(self, "baselines"): merged = context_df.join(self.baselines, on=["entity_id", "context_band"]) out["context_z"] = ((merged["value"] - merged["median"]) / merged["std"].clip(lower=1e-6)) out.loc[merged["count"] < 30, "context_z"] = np.nan # insufficient history return out ``` Four design decisions worth calling out. **`RobustScaler`** rather than `StandardScaler`, because the training data contains the outliers you are looking for. **Rank normalisation** before averaging, since raw scores from different methods live on incompatible scales. **Contextual z-scores alongside** the global ensemble, because the two catch different things. And **an explicit minimum-history guard**, so a machine with eight readings does not generate spurious contextual alerts. Operational requirements that separate a working system from a demo: **Monitor the alert rate.** A sudden spike usually means an upstream data change, not a real surge in anomalies. **Feed investigated alerts back as labels.** After six months you have enough to train a supervised model, which will substantially outperform any unsupervised detector. **Retrain on a schedule**, because normal drifts. A detector trained on 2024 behaviour flags all of 2026 as anomalous. **Explain every alert.** Per-feature contributions turn "score 0.94" into "vibration is 4.2 standard deviations above this machine's baseline", which is what an engineer can act on. ##### Common mistakes - A single global threshold on data where anomalies are contextual. - Plain z-scores on contaminated data, where masking hides the outliers. - `StandardScaler` before detection, when the outliers corrupt the scaling parameters. - Treating `contamination` as a model parameter rather than a threshold setting. - Confusing LOF's `novelty=True` and `novelty=False` modes. - Training an autoencoder on data containing the anomalies you want to detect. - An autoencoder bottleneck wide enough to learn the identity function. - Reporting accuracy on a problem with 0.2% anomalies. - Averaging raw scores from methods with incompatible scales. - Never retraining, so drift makes everything look anomalous. ##### Hands-on Apply a statistical method, Isolation Forest and LOF to a dataset with known anomalies. Compare which anomalies each catches by building the overlap matrix — the disagreements are the informative part, because they reveal what each method is structurally able to see. Evaluate with precision-recall on the labelled subset and report precision@k for a realistic review capacity. Then construct a contextual anomaly that all three global methods miss, and show that a per-entity baseline catches it. For the mini-project, build an anomaly detection system for a realistic scenario — fraud, sensor faults or data-quality monitoring. Combine at least two complementary methods with rank-normalised ensemble scoring, add contextual baselines with a minimum-history guard, and tune the threshold against an explicit cost matrix rather than a percentile. Include an evaluation section using whatever labels you have plus synthetic injection and consensus analysis, an explanation layer producing per-feature contributions for each alert, and a monitoring plan covering alert-rate tracking and retraining cadence. Report expected annual value against the current rule if one exists. For the assignment, give a concrete example of a contextual anomaly and explain why a simple global threshold would miss it. Use real numbers, state what the global threshold was, what the contextual baseline was, and what the cost of the miss turned out to be. The gearbox is the template; find or construct your own. ##### Key takeaways - Most expensive anomalies are contextual, and most deployed systems only detect point anomalies — that gap is where failures live. - Use robust statistics (MAD, IQR, MinCovDet) because the outliers you are hunting corrupt the mean and covariance. - Isolation Forest is the scalable default; LOF catches local density anomalies; autoencoders handle high-dimensional and sequential data. - Train autoencoders and novelty detectors on clean data only, and keep the bottleneck narrow. - With few labels, combine synthetic injection, cross-method consensus and expert review of the top k — and set the threshold from cost, not a percentile.
